text:
One-liner:
print(max((input().split() for _ in range(int(input()))), key=lambda x: x[1])[0])

Your approach can be simplified. You do not need to store the items in a list; rather, you can process each item before the next is input:
max_enjoyment = -1
num_f = int(input())
for i in range(num_f):
    name, enjoyment = input().split()
    enjoyment = int(enjoyment)
    if enjoyment > max_enjoyment:
        max_enjoyment = enjoyment
        winner = name
print(winner)

text:
As you’ve discovered, adding the names and the values to the same list, but as separate items, makes it harder to work with that list.  Why not do
num_f = int(input())
list_f = []
for i in range(num_f):
    name, enjoyment = input().split()
    enjoyment = int(enjoyment)
    list_f.append((enjoyment, name))

And because I put the enjoyment value first, I can compare the items directly, so this works:
winner_enjoyment, winner_name = max(list_f)
print(winner_name)
author: mgedmin

text: The tuple-ordering approach is the clean part here. Storing (enjoyment, name) means max() compares the integer first and only falls back to the name on ties, which is usually what you want. The one-liner fails because x[1] is still a string, so comparisons are lexicographic, and the indexing assumes a shape the generator doesn’t produce. Unpacking into named variables also makes the result readable. Reshaping the data early beats fighting it later.
